item.title: Multimodal neuroimaging fusion with interpretable deep learning for speech motor dysfunction in Parkinson's disease.
item.description:
PLOS digital health
Speech motor dysfunction affects approximately 90% of patients with Parkinson's disease (PD), but multimodal neuroimaging models for prediction of this impairment remain limited. We developed MCTA-FusNet, an interpretable deep learning framework that integrates structural, resting-state functional, and diffusion MRI to predict speech motor dysfunction in PD. The model incorporates modality-specific encoders and a hierarchical triple-attention fusion mechanism to capture channel-, spatial-, and modality-level interactions. Using cross-domain transfer learning, MCTA-FusNet was first pretrained on the PPMI dataset (n = 400) to predict motor symptom severity (UPDRS-III) and then fine-tuned on the FAH-SYSU dataset (n = 81) to predict speech motor dysfunction, indexed by vocal response magnitude (VRMag) to pitch perturbations. MCTA-FusNet outperformed all unimodal and multimodal models with transfer learning, achieving the lowest mean absolute error (1.388 ± 0.62) and highest correlation between predicted and observed VRMag (r = 0.731, p < 0.001). Interpretability analyses identified the superior temporal gyrus, primary motor cortex, premotor cortex, and supplementary motor area as key predictors, with greater coherence and phase synchrony between auditory and premotor regions significantly correlated with exaggerated VRMag. These findings establish a multimodal neuroimaging deep learning model for predicting and explaining speech motor dysfunction in PD, offering a novel framework with potential for symptom-specific monitoring and therapeutic intervention.

item.title: Differential vulnerability of stimulus-locked and persistent gamma oscillations: Implications in schizophrenia.
item.description:
PLoS computational biology
Working memory depends on gamma oscillations generated across sensory and prefrontal cortices. In primary visual cortex (V1), stimulus-locked gamma oscillations encode stimulus information, while in prefrontal cortex (PFC), persistent gamma oscillations maintain this information after the stimulus is removed. In schizophrenia (SZ), gamma power is reduced in both V1 and PFC, consistent with deficits in sensory encoding and working memory maintenance. Both oscillation regimes arise from a canonical microcircuit involving pyramidal neurons (PNs) and parvalbumin-expressing interneurons (PVIs). Yet, whether the two regimes are similarly or differentially vulnerable to synaptic alterations within this circuit in SZ remains unknown. To investigate this question, we used a mean-field model of the PN-PVI circuit, in which the two regimes were distinguished by NMDA conductance values reflecting the difference in GluN2B expression between human PFC and V1. We then assessed three synaptic alterations quantified using molecular and structural proxies in postmortem SZ brains: lower excitatory inputs to PVIs (E→I), lower inhibitory inputs to PNs (I→E), and greater variability in E→I strength. Each alteration produced larger gamma power deficits in the persistent regime than in the stimulus-locked regime. Applied together, these alterations interacted synergistically to reduce gamma power, with the persistent regime exhibiting a more pronounced deficit. Bifurcation analyses revealed that this differential vulnerability arises from a wider margin of oscillatory stability in the stimulus-locked regime, and that reduced I→E strength additionally abolished the bistability required for the persistent regime. These findings predict that a larger magnitude of synaptic alteration is required to disrupt gamma oscillations in V1 than in PFC, consistent with postmortem reports of more severe alterations in V1 in SZ. Together, they establish a differential vulnerability model of cortical gamma oscillations in SZ, in which regional differences in oscillatory stability determine how much synaptic alteration is required to disrupt oscillations with distinct dynamics.

item.title: Neuropathologic Correlates of Cognitive Decline in Community-Dwelling Elders Who Die as Centenarians.
item.description:
Neurology
BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Brain pathologies are common in the elderly; however, their contribution to Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in those who die as centenarians remain unclear. This study examines the frequency of Alzheimer disease neuropathologic changes (ADNC), limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy neuropathologic change (LATE-NC), and other brain pathologies and their association with Alzheimer dementia risk and cognitive decline in centenarians. METHODS: This clinicopathologic study included older participants from the Religious Orders Study and Rush Memory and Aging Project, 2 ongoing clinicopathologic cohort studies of aging and dementia, who underwent annual clinical evaluations and autopsy. Participants were evaluated annually for cognitive status and followed for a mean (SD) of 11.4 (5.3) years before death. Neuropathologic evaluation included ADNC (and separately β-amyloid load and tangle density), LATE-NC, presence or absence of neocortical Lewy bodies (LBs), hippocampal sclerosis of aging (HS-A), primary age-related tauopathy (PART), and 5 cerebrovascular disease (CVD) pathologies including arteriolosclerosis, atherosclerosis, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, macroinfarcts, and microinfarcts. Multivariable regression and linear mixed-effects models were applied. RESULTS: A total of 104 centenarians were included in this study. The mean (SD) age at death was 102 (1.9) years, 84% were female, 58% had Alzheimer dementia, 21% had mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 21% had no cognitive impairment (NCI). All 3 clinical diagnostic groups exhibited pathologies, including any type of CVD (94%), ADNC (72%; 73% of them were intermediate and 27% of them were high), LATE-NC (58%, 30% of them exhibiting HS-A), HS-A (18%, 95% had LATE-NC), PART (28%), and neocortical LBs (11%). Mixed pathologies, particularly ADNC + LATE-NC + CVD, were common in the Alzheimer dementia group (52%) compared with NCI (36%) and MCI (23%). After adjusted for age at death, sex, education, and other brain pathologies, only LATE-NC and tangles (specifically intermediate/high ADNC with Braak stage V) were associated with more rapid decline in global cognition and increased odds of Alzheimer dementia. DISCUSSION: Brain pathology, but not dementia, is nearly inevitable in those who die as centenarians. LATE-NC and tangles are the key contributors to cognitive decline. Future study investigating resilience factors may inform preventive strategies.

item.title: Predictors of Recovery From Aphasia After Stroke.
item.description:
Stroke
Predicting recovery from aphasia after stroke is challenging, yet essential. Accurate prognoses would enable stroke survivors and families to establish realistic expectations and make informed decisions, allow clinicians to plan rehabilitation, and inform the development and implementation of interventions. This review synthesizes current evidence on predictors of aphasia recovery, integrating diverse biological, behavioral, environmental, and temporal determinants into a unified conceptual framework organized around 3 fundamental determinants: the integrity of the language network, neuroplasticity throughout the remaining brain, and the passage of time. Lesion location and extent are powerful predictors, accounting for more than half of the variance in aphasia outcomes, but other interacting factors contribute to heterogeneous recovery trajectories, including variability in language network organization and effects of diaschisis. The capacity for neuroplasticity depends on the brain health and functionality of surviving tissue, but the realization of this potential depends critically on engagement in language use, which can be promoted by intensive speech-language therapy, social participation and supportive communication environments. Recovery follows a predictable decelerating time course, with rapid early gains driven primarily by reperfusion and resolution of dysfunction in brain regions that support language, and modest but meaningful longer-term improvements deriving from neuroplastic changes. This framework provides a practical heuristic for understanding aphasia recovery, developing clinical prediction tools, and identifying modifiable factors to optimize outcomes.

item.title: Altered Intrinsic Brain Network Organization in Inflammatory Bowel Disease: Differential Associations with Pain Sensitivity and Perceived Stress.
item.description:
Neuroimmunomodulation
INTRODUCTION: The persistence of abdominal pain and related gastrointestinal symptoms despite disease remission suggests that inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) may involve central alterations that extend beyond periods of active intestinal inflammation. Yet, intrinsic brain network organization in ulcerative colitis (UC) remains insufficiently characterized, particularly in relation to factors relevant to symptom persistence, such as pain sensitivity and chronic stress burden. We therefore investigated resting-state functional connectivity (FC) within the default mode network (DMN) and salience network in UC and examined associations with heat pain thresholds and perceived chronic stress. METHODS: Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data from 17 female patients with UC and 19 female healthy controls (HC) were analyzed using group-level independent component analysis. FC differences within the identified DMN and salience network components were assessed in a priori defined regions of interest implicated in interoceptive and affective pain-related processing. Associations between altered FC and heat pain thresholds as well as perceived chronic stress were examined. RESULTS: Patients with UC differed from HC in the intrinsic organization of both the DMN and salience network. DMN alterations included increased FC of the posterior insula and medial superior frontal gyrus, alongside decreased FC of the dorsolateral superior frontal gyrus. Salience network alterations involved increased FC of the anterior insula, midcingulate cortex, and orbital inferior frontal gyrus. In UC, stronger FC of the anterior insula and orbital inferior frontal gyrus within the salience network was associated with lower heat pain thresholds, corresponding to greater experimental pain sensitivity. These associations were absent in HC. Connectivity of the orbital inferior frontal gyrus was additionally associated with perceived chronic stress in HC, but not in UC. CONCLUSION: UC is characterized by altered intrinsic organization of brain networks central to interoceptive and affective pain-related processing. The association between stronger salience network connectivity and greater experimental pain sensitivity suggests that central network alterations may be involved in pain-related mechanisms beyond acute intestinal inflammation. These findings highlight the potential clinical relevance of considering central pain mechanisms alongside peripheral inflammation to better understand persistent pain in IBD.

item.title: Hyperactivity of the posterior cingulate cortex during interpreting communicative intentions based on the speaker-listener relationship in autism spectrum disorder.
item.description:
Social neuroscience
Speakers' intended meanings are often inferred from extra-linguistic social factors such as the speaker-listener relationship, yet how individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) incorporate such relational cues remains unclear. Using fMRI, we investigated whether and how individuals with autism utilize speaker-listener relationship cues to interpret communicative intentions. Twenty adults with ASD and 20 matched typically developed (TD) controls completed a discourse comprehension task where the interpretation of a target remark depended on the speaker-listener relationship or not. Behaviorally, both groups showed faster reactions in the social factor condition, indicating that the social context facilitated their responses. However, the ASD group was less accurate overall. Across the groups, core discourse regions, including the medial prefrontal cortex and inferior frontal gyrus, were engaged. Critically, ASD participants exhibited increased activation in the posterior cingulate cortex (PCC), whereas TD participants showed PCC deactivation. Functional connectivity analyses further indicated reduced PCC connectivity with the left angular gyrus and right fusiform gyrus in ASD compared with TD. These findings suggest that, despite broadly comparable task engagement, individuals with ASD rely on different PCC-centered neural mechanisms when integrating speaker-listener relationship information to infer communicative intentions.

item.title: Content-related motor cortical representation during attempted handwriting.
item.description:
Cell reports
Humans are superb at handwriting, and we can write in diverse ways, such as with a pen or with a fingertip. Remarkably, although different ways of writing involve divergent muscle activations, we can easily transfer our writing skill from one way to another without deliberate practice. Here, we investigated the neural substrates of this phenomenon by recording single-unit activity from the human motor cortex (MC) while a paralyzed participant attempted to write the same symbols under three effector conditions. Our results show that MC activity contains both content-related and effector-related information. Population analyses further indicate a content-related neural latent space shared across effector conditions. These findings suggest that a shared content-related subspace preserves writing content information across effector conditions and supports cross-effector decoding.

item.title: Poorer inhibition and switching are associated with lower white matter fibre density in the superior longitudinal fasciculus in groups clinically at-risk of probable Alzheimer's disease dementia.
item.description:
Journal of neurology
Executive dysfunction and white matter microstructural alterations in the superior longitudinal fasciculus (SLF) may occur in the clinically defined at-risk groups of Alzheimer's disease (AD) dementia and be potentially useful and early markers of risk. We used diffusion-weighted MRI and fixel-based analysis to investigate inhibition/switching executive functioning and white matter properties of three SLF subdivisions (SLF 1, SLF 2, SLF 3) in groups clinically at-risk of AD-dementia: controls (C; n = 35), subjective cognitive decline (SCD; n = 60), single-domain amnestic mild cognitive impairment (aMCI; n = 55), and multiple-domain amnestic MCI (mMCI; n = 52). Individuals with probable AD-dementia (n = 27) were also compared with controls. Linear trend analyses showed increasingly poorer executive functioning performance and lower fibre density (FD) in the right SLF 2 and bilateral SLF 3 across groups. Analysis of covariance (age, sex) revealed SCD and mMCI groups had lower FD bilaterally in the SLF 3 than controls. The AD-dementia group showed more extensively reduced FD in four of the six SLF divisions, and lower fibre density cross-section (FDC) in five of the six SLF divisions than controls. Partial least-squares (PLS) analyses showed that poorer executive functioning, but not processing speed, was associated with lower FD in the SLF in the at-risk sample. This pattern was also found in AD-dementia/controls PLS, which additionally showed this association with FDC. Collectively, our results implicate altered microstructural fibre properties in the SLF and poorer executive functioning in groups at risk of AD-dementia, with FD changes in SLF present in SCD, prior to objective cognitive decline.

item.title: Regional cortical thickness differences between progressive and stable mild cognitive impairment.
item.description:
Experimental brain research
Accurately differentiating progressive mild cognitive impairment (pMCI) from stable mild cognitive impairment (sMCI) may help characterize individuals with different patterns of cognitive progression toward Alzheimer's disease (AD). This 24-month MRI study aimed to compare regional cortical thickness and hemispheric asymmetry between the pMCI and sMCI groups. A total of 40 participants, including 20 with sMCI and 20 with pMCI, were selected from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) database. For each participant, baseline and 24-month follow-up T1-weighted MRI scans were analyzed. Cortical thickness measurements were performed using FreeSurfer software, and bilaterally averaged regional cortical thickness values were analyzed using ANCOVA to assess group differences in baseline-adjusted follow-up cortical thickness, asymmetry, and laterality indices. To correct for multiple comparisons, the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied at an FDR of 0.10. The pMCI group exhibited significantly lower baseline-adjusted follow-up cortical thickness than the sMCI group in the inferior temporal, middle temporal, parahippocampal, and fusiform gyri. No significant between-group differences were observed in the Asymmetry Index or Laterality Index. Overall, these findings suggest that regional cortical thickness may provide useful information on structural differences between pMCI and sMCI, particularly in temporal regions.

item.title: Brain cycle flexibility and behavioral association
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Canonical models of the macroscopic human connectome are dominated through static, cortico-centric networks by positive functional correlates. Yet naturalistic behavior demands fluid topological reconfigurations, wherein biologically critical functional antagonism (negative correlates) is routinely discarded as noise. Meanwhile, deep subcortical control remains overlooked. Here, we develop the Spatial Connectivity Cycle Flexibility (SCCF) framework to track whole-brain community dynamics across signed interactions. We show that canonical static networks reflect time-averaged projections of an underlying dynamic probability landscape, actively orchestrated by three (basal, regulatory, and fast) conserved subcortical routing modes. Individual dynamic modular co-occurrence function-prints predict 16 independent behavioral dimensions across cognitive, personality, and physiological domains, indicating that behavioral heterogeneity depends on the dynamic balance between network integration and antagonistic segregation. Crucially, independent cross-cohort validation reveals an organizational duality: subcortical routing for core cognitive computation is broadly conserved across cultures, whereas socio-emotional circuits exhibit marked divergence aligned with distinct behavioral ecologies. These findings challenge prevailing cortico-centric and positive-only assumptions of the functional connectome, providing an exploratory computational framework that links subcortical routing and active network antagonism to human phenotypic diversity and behavioral adaptation.

item.title: Being Born versus Being Born Early: Disentangling Birth from Prematurity in Perinatal Brain Development
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Studies of preterm birth report both delayed and accelerated brain maturation, depending on whether preterm infants are compared with term newborns or with fetuses. We propose that these mixed observations arise because such comparisons conflate two distinct influences, the effect of birth on term-aged infants and the independent effects of being born prematurely. Using MRI data from 330 term and 118 preterm neonates in the developing Human Connectome Project (dHCP), we developed a simple piecewise linear model that estimates prenatal and postnatal rates of development separately for term and preterm infants across volumetric, microstructural and connectivity measures. In term infants, birth accelerated volumetric growth, with total brain volume growing 44\% faster post-birth, with regionally specific alterations in microstructural trajectories. Deep white matter continued to mature, whereas superficial and cerebellar white matter reversed direction. Changes in cortical connectivity at birth followed the sensorimotor to association axis, shifting towards specialisation in sensory and insular cortex and towards more diverse connectivity in association cortex. In contrast, the effect of birth on preterm infants was much weaker, where development largely continued at prenatal rates. These results show that the impact of birth depends on brain region and maturational state at birth. Separating birth from prematurity offers a framework for interpreting mixed findings in the perinatal literature.

item.title: Feature processing for single-trial semantic decoding from EEG: a factorial comparison with pre-registered replication
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Single-trial decoding of semantic processing from EEG is used in cognitive neuroscience, brain–computer interfaces and EEG-to-text research. Because single trials are noisy, the choice of features can determine how much information a decoder uses. Yet these fields use different features that have not been compared systematically: event-related potential studies decode the voltage time course (the waveform), EEG-to-text studies mostly the power of oscillations in frequency bands. We crossed four feature-processing choices—signal representation (waveform or band power), time window, normalization and channel set—into 640 configurations and decoded whether a stimulus fitted its semantic context in three tasks: visual word pairs, objects in visual scenes, and words in spoken sentences (40 participants per task). Eleven pre-specified comparisons were tested jointly. The signal representation had by far the largest effect on accuracy (mean generalized eta squared = 0.165, an order of magnitude above any other effect). Averaged over tasks and other choices, balanced accuracy was 56.6% with the waveform and 50.6% with theta-band power (chance, 50%), and adding band power to the waveform lowered accuracy by 1.8 percentage points, in every task. Both effects replicated, and were larger, in a pre-registered study of 283 new participants from three sites. Neither a finer time–frequency decomposition including the delta band (2–4 Hz) nor a different way of combining power with the waveform changed this conclusion, whereas the time window, normalization and channel set mattered little. For semantic decoding from single EEG trials, the waveform carries the information, and band power does not add to it.

item.title: Shared Neural Dynamics of Sentence-Level Language Processing in Verbally Proficient Autistic and Non-Autistic Adults
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Autistic individuals often show atypical language development during childhood, yet many attain typical language proficiency by adulthood. This raises the question of whether the neural processes supporting language differ in autism once language has been acquired. Using electroencephalography (EEG), we compared verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults during rapid serial visual presentation of structured sentences and pseudoword lists. Sentence processing elicited oscillatory responses across theta, alpha, beta, and gamma frequency bands, with distinct spatiotemporal profiles and hemispheric lateralization most pronounced in the theta, alpha, and beta bands. Notably, beta-band activity increased over sentence position and was positively associated with verbal ability, consistent with a role in the maintenance and integration of linguistic information. These effects were highly comparable across groups, with similar patterns observed at both the individual and group levels and across sensor- and source-level analyses. Together, these findings indicate largely shared neural dynamics of sentence-level language processing in verbally proficient autistic and non-autistic adults, suggesting that atypical language-related neural organization is not an inevitable feature of autism in adulthood.

item.title: The language network responds stronger to connected than to unconnected sentences
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Purpose: Reliable functional mapping of the language network and preoperative assessment of language lateralization are essential for safe and effective craniotomy in patients with lesions in language‑eloquent brain regions, yet existing fMRI language paradigms are often time‑consuming and place substantial cognitive and economic demands on patients and diagnostic services. Methods: We therefore tested ecologically valid German stimulus sets designed to optimize measurement efficiency. Forty-three healthy participants (mean age = 38 years, range = 20 - 64; 24 women) were scanned on a 3T MRI while reading or listening to 4-, 8-, and 12-word sentences and pseudoword lists or texts, each followed by a decision task. Sentences were selected from German literary classics and text passages from general-interest science magazines and matched across conditions for lexical and structural properties. Results: Region‑of‑interest analyses in subject‑specific, functionally defined language‑sensitive regions showed robust activation of the left‑hemispheric language network across modalities. Within participants, texts elicited significantly larger effect sizes than sentences, and longer sentences generally produced stronger responses than shorter ones. Task manipulations expected to increase cognitive demand (short 4‑word sentences with frequent probes, coherent texts requiring deeper semantic integration) did not enhance responses in the domain‑general multiple demand network, indicating that executive‑control activity did not overshadow language‑selective activation, whereas substantial overlap between default mode and language‑sensitive regions in the left temporal lobe was consistent with relatively automatic processing of connected language. Conclusions: These findings indicate that ecologically valid sentence‑ and text‑based paradigms can provide efficient, language‑specific fMRI protocols for preoperative diagnostics and individualized presurgical planning in patients with lesions near language‑eloquent cortex.

item.title: Resting-State Imaging of Vestibular Migraine:Integrative Insights from Amplitude,Homogeneity,and Functional Connection.
item.description:
Zhongguo yi xue ke xue yuan xue bao. Acta Academiae Medicinae Sinicae
Vestibular migraine (VM) represents a prevalent central vestibular disorder characterized by episodic vertigo and migraine attacks,yet its neuropathological basis remains poorly understood.Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging has emerged as a valuable investigative tool for identifying central network dysfunction in VM,given its sensitivity in detecting spontaneous brain activity.Drawing on seed-based functional connectivity studies and measures including amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations,fractional amplitude of low-frequency fluctuations,and regional homogeneity,this review examines aberrant spontaneous activity in VM patients across the thalamus,cerebellum,frontoparietal cortex,and insula.Key pathological circuits include disrupted vestibular-thalamo-cortical projections,dysregulated pain-emotion processing networks,and compensatory recruitment of visual-spatial attention and motor pathways.These findings furnish important neuroimaging evidence for understanding the pathophysiology and identifying the potential diagnostic and therapeutic biomarkers for VM.

item.title: The Inferior Parietal Lobule Links Childhood Trauma to Non-Suicidal Self- Injury via Anxiety
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Background Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) refers to deliberate self-harm without suicidal intent, and the neural mechanisms underlying disturbed bodily self-consciousness (BSC) in NSSI remain unclear. This study examined cortical thickness across BSC-related regions and their mediating role in the childhood trauma–NSSI relationship. Methods A total of 173 young participants (aged 10–24 years) were classified into NSSI (n = 117) and non-NSSI (n = 56) groups based on DSM-5 criteria; structural MRI data with complete surface-quality metrics were available for 128. Cortical thickness was measured bilaterally in five BSC regions: inferior parietal lobule (IPL), supramarginal gyrus, insula, postcentral gyrus, and posterior cingulate cortex. ANCOVA with permutation-based inference and FDR correction, serial mediation analyses with bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals, and an exploratory whole-cortex analysis across 34 regions were conducted. Results Only the IPL exhibited significant group differences after FDR correction (p = 0.010, pFDR = 0.049; d = − 0.42), with the NSSI group displaying thinner cortex; in the whole-cortex analysis, the IPL showed the largest cortical thinning of all 34 regions. Childhood trauma correlated with thinner IPL (r = − 0.19, p = 0.039). Serial mediation revealed a significant indirect pathway from childhood trauma to NSSI through IPL thickness and anxiety (indirect effect = 0.012, 95% CI [0.001, 0.040]); the anxiety-alone pathway was more substantial (34.3%), and full mediation was observed. Conclusions Among the five BSC regions, only the IPL was associated with NSSI. Altered higher-order body representation may constitute a neural pathway linking early adversity to NSSI through heightened anxiety.

item.title: Anterior Cingulate Cortex Metabolism, Microstructure, and Social Withdrawal in Autism Spectrum Disorder
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract The anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) supports social behavior, which can be normalized by manipulating ACC function in animal models of autism spectrum disorder (ASD). How ACC metabolism and microstructure jointly relate to social behavior in humans with ASD remains unclear. Proton magnetic resonance spectroscopy measured glutamate (Glu), glutamine (Gln), lactate (Lac), and myo-inositol (Ins), while neurite orientation dispersion and density imaging estimated neurite density index (NDI) and orientation dispersion index (ODI) in the same ACC voxel in 96 adults with ASD and 63 typically developing controls (TDC). Analyses included group comparisons, partial correlations, networks, and permutation-based dimensional models incorporating Japanese Autism-Spectrum Quotient (AQ-J), 25-item Hikikomori Questionnaire (HQ-25), and diagnosis, plus an ASD-only sensitivity analysis using the validated HQ-25 cutoff. ACC Lac was higher in ASD, but the difference was not significant after multiple-comparison correction; Glu, Gln, and Ins did not differ significantly between groups. Four network edges were retained in ASD, with bootstrap support for Glu–Ins and Gln–Lac; none were retained in TDC. Glu correlated significantly with lower NDI and higher ODI only in ASD. HQ-25—but neither AQ-J nor diagnosis—showed significant positive associations with Lac, Glu, and Gln. The ASD-only sensitivity analysis corroborated the Lac association. Altered ACC metabolic–structural coupling in ASD, possibly reflecting astrocytic dysfunction, may be informative beyond concentration differences alone. Metabolite associations with social withdrawal, independent of general autistic traits, suggest a behavioral dimension relevant to precision medicine in ASD.

item.title: Adiposity in Adolescence has Detrimental Effects on Developing Brain Structures and Organization, Communication, and Controllability of Resting-State Networks
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Adiposity in adolescence can have detrimental effects on neural maturation, and is associated with incompletely understood alterations in brain structures and circuits. To address this important knowledge gap, N = 3,341 youth from the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) two-year follow-up cohort (median(IQR) age = 12.0(1.1) years; 51.0% females), with structural MRI and resting-state fMRI were studied. Topological properties reflecting network strength, resilience, efficiency and modularity, information transfer, regional feedback costs associated with controllability of network dynamics, and morphometric characteristics were examined as a function of body mass index (BMI), body roundness index (BRI), overweight, obesity, and persistent excess BMI (across assessments). Youth who slept less, spent more time on electronic devices, were Hispanic and/or from lower-income families had higher BMI/BRI (β = 0.07–4.95, 95%CI=[0.03,7.05]), and higher odds of overweight or obesity (aOR = 1.01–1.72, 95%CI=[1.01,2.28]). Higher BMI/BRI, overweight, obesity and/or persistent excess BMI were associated with weaker and less resilient networks supporting decision-making, control, emotional regulation, reward processing and social function (β=-0.11 to -0.01, CI=[-0.16,-0.01]), and more topologically fragile thalamus and basal ganglia (β = 0.05–0.10, CI=[0.01,0.14], p < 0.03). They were also associated with lower control costs in cognitive and topological hubs (including the precuneus and prefrontal regions) that play central roles in regulating brain dynamics, aberrant information transfer in limbic, frontoparietal, salience, somatomotor and cerebellar regions, and lower thickness and/or volume of distributed (including prefrontal) regions, and functional hubs (β=-0.14 to -0.02, CI=[-0.18,-0.01]). Thus, adiposity in adolescence is associated with widespread structural and alterations of brain networks supporting developing cognitive processes, and fundamental mechanisms that control these networks’ dynamics.

item.title: Neural Signatures of Predictive Processing during Natural Mandarin Speech Comprehension.
item.description:
eNeuro
Language comprehension requires the continuous transformation of speech into a hierarchy of linguistic units, from phonemes to syllables to words. Because speech unfolds rapidly, listeners are thought to predict upcoming content to keep pace. Previous research has provided empirical evidence for predictive processes operating at multiple linguistic levels during naturalistic listening, including words and phonemes. However, it remains unclear whether prediction also operates concurrently at other levels, such as syllabic and phrasal representation. Here we use Mandarin Chinese to examine the neural signatures of predictive processing across multiple levels of linguistic granularity during natural speech comprehension. Mandarin comprises four representational levels: phoneme, sub-syllabic, character and word, and its lexical identity is largely constrained at the sub-syllabic level, potentially redistributing predictive weight across linguistic representations. We recorded magnetoencephalography (MEG) data while 34 native Mandarin speakers (21 females) listened to a naturalistic audiobook and applied linear regression modeling to examine how linguistic features modulated neural activity. We found that the brain activity of listeners segmented speech into hierarchical units, and that surprisal modulated responses simultaneously across sub-syllabic, character and word levels. In contrast to findings from Indo-European languages, however, we did not observe unique surprisal effects at the lowest, phonemic level. Furthermore, the surprisal of lexical tone in Mandarin modulated brain activity only when integrated with its phonological components. These findings suggest that predictive processing during Mandarin speech comprehension operates concurrently across multiple (though not necessarily all) levels of linguistic granularity, with its implementation shaped by language-specific structural properties.Significance statement Language comprehension involves segmenting a continuous acoustic stream into multiple linguistic units, from phonemes to words, and generating predictions at these levels. However, direct neural evidence remains limited regarding how segmentation and prediction operate simultaneously across levels of linguistic granularity, particularly outside Indo-European languages. Using temporal response function analysis of magnetoencephalography data recorded during naturalistic Mandarin listening, we show that predictive processing occurs across multiple levels of linguistic granularity. Specifically, we find evidence for prediction-related neural responses at sub-syllabic, character, and word levels, but not a reliable unique effect at the phonemic level. These results indicate that predictive processing also operates during Mandarin speech comprehension, and its neural implementation is shaped by language-specific structural properties.

item.title: Exploring prefrontal mitochondrial metabolism and its coupling with hemoxygenation as biomarkers for cognition and psychopathology: A pilot fNIRS study.
item.description:
Neuroimmunomodulation
Cerebral mitochondrial dysregulation and altered neurometabolic coupling have been implicated across psychiatric and neurocognitive disorders. However, in vivo human data assessing these mechanisms within a transdiagnostic framework remain limited. We investigated left frontopolar mitochondrial metabolism, blood oxygenation, and their coupling at rest and during cognitive tasks in relation to general psychopathology (p) and general cognition (g). In a transdiagnostic sample of 65 adults (n=50 included after quality control), changes in mitochondrial metabolism (Δ[oxCCO]) and blood oxygenation (Δ[HbD]) were measured at the left frontal pole (Fp1) using single-channel broadband functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Three mitochondrial-hemoxygenation coupling indices were computed: relative power (rPwr), relative cost (rCst) and intraindividual distance correlation. Outcomes included composite factors for general psychopathology (p, derived from validated self-report questionnaires) and general cognition (g, derived from four cognitive tasks). Primary confirmatory hypotheses were not confirmed: task-evoked mitochondrial metabolism and interindividual coupling markers (rPwr, rCst) showed no significant associations with p or g, nor did they differentiate diagnostic status groups (p > 0.05). In exploratory analyses, a higher intraindividual task-evoked mitochondrial-hemoxygenation correlation was associated with higher g (r = 0.44, p = 0.008; n = 35). Conversely, higher resting-state Δ[oxCCO] and Δ[HbD] were associated with lower g (r = -0.58 and r = -0.55, both p ≤ 0.001; n = 31). Associations with general psychopathology were not statistically significant. While primary confirmatory hypotheses were rejected, exploratory findings provide preliminary evidence that prefrontal mitochondrial-hemoxygenation coupling (both at rest and during cognitive engagement) is relevant to cognitive functioning. Given the pilot nature and data loss constraints, this non-invasive broadband fNIRS approach warrants validation in larger, adequately powered confirmatory studies.

item.title: A shared meaning component across languages in the human brain.
item.description:
Nature neuroscience
Human languages differ profoundly in their sounds, words and grammatical systems, yet all support the communication of complex meanings. How the brain handles this diversity remains a fundamental question in language neuroscience. Multilingual neural network models offer a way to answer this question by representing linguistic content across languages in a shared space. Leveraging these advances, we evaluated the similarity of linguistic representations in speakers of 21 languages. Here we combined existing (12 languages across 4 language families) and newly collected functional magnetic resonance imaging data (9 languages across 4 families) to test encoding models predicting brain activity in the language network using representations from multilingual models. Model representations predicted brain responses reliably within each language. Critically, encoding models trained on one set of languages generalized zero-shot to previously unseen languages, accurately predicting neural responses without exposure to the target language. This cross-lingual generalization extended across variation in language family, stimulus type and presentation modality. These findings point to a shared cross-lingual component for meaning across human languages.

item.title: Linguistic contextualization in the human hippocampus.
item.description:
Nature human behaviour
Word meanings in language are contextualized by surrounding words. Inspired by the self-attention mechanism in transformer-based large language models (LLMs), we hypothesized that structural composition in the brain arises from combining canonical (non-contextual) word representations with those of nearby words. We analysed single unit activity in the human hippocampus, a region involved in semantic and contextual processing, while n = 10 participants listened to podcasts. We found that hippocampal neurons encoded word position within a clause, using both ordinal and frequency-domain positional encoding. Moreover, neural responses to specific words reflected both the lexical semantics of the word and a weighted sum of the embeddings of preceding words. The relative weighting of these contextualizing words correlated with LLM self-attention weights. These findings suggest that contextualization in the brain makes use of vectorial shifts that have a resemblance to attentional reweighting in LLMs, and highlight the role of the mesial temporal lobe within the broader language network.

item.title: Biophysical brain twins map the phenotype-expotype architecture of ageing and dementia.
item.description:
Nature biomedical engineering
Biophysical whole-brain models may reveal causal links between neural dynamics and biological-environmental variation, yet no framework has explained how these factors become embedded in mechanistic dynamics. Here we develop individualized biophysical digital twins mechanistically linked to phenotypes and expotypes (that is, combinations of exposomal influences) leveraging resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data (n = 6,986, 16 countries) of healthy controls and participants with mild cognitive impairment, Alzheimer's disease and frontotemporal dementia. Personalized twins improved goodness-of-fit over group-level models. They reproduced structure-function coupling between regional excitability and brain volume, captured age, sex and neurodegeneration, and encoded 68 expotypes. Associations remained robust after controlling for demographics, data quality, model fit and scanner/site, with the strongest effects for social and physical (pollution) exposomes. We release an open resource (empirical data, code, >3 million simulations) for future research. These findings ground phenotypic-exposomic variation in individualized biophysical twins, enabling in silico testing of mechanisms and potential model-informed interventions.

item.title: Spatiotemporal brain dynamics of limb ownership perception.
item.description:
Nature communications
We experience our limbs as our own, but how does the brain generate this fundamental sense of body ownership? Previous studies have relied mainly on fMRI or lesion mapping, providing a static view of the neural mechanisms underlying body ownership. Using magnetoencephalography, robotically controlled visuotactile stimulation, and multivariate analysis across the rubber hand illusion, a real hand condition, and multiple control conditions, we identified source vector dissimilarity patterns reflecting ownership of the left arm. Three phases of ownership-specific activity patterns emerged: (i) anticipatory patterns in medial frontal cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and right posterior cerebellum before tactile stimulation; (ii) multisensory integration patterns in right dorsal and ventral premotor cortex, right posterior parietal cortex, and anterior cerebellum at 116-156 ms poststimulus; and (iii) later bilateral insular and left hemisphere patterns at 184-232 ms. These findings provide a whole-brain, time-resolved map of activity patterns underlying body ownership, revealing its dynamic neural construction.

item.title: Manipulating speech perception with amplitude-modulated kilohertz magnetic perturbation (AM-kTMP).
item.description:
Brain stimulation
Speech perception has been hypothesized to exploit neural activity that entrains to the rhythmic properties of the utterance. Perceptual sensitivity varies with the phase of oscillatory activity induced by speech, and with an external oscillatory perturbation induced by transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS) over the temporal lobe. However, current non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) methods suffer from limitations that include peripheral nerve stimulation and hinder neural entrainment research. Here we used a new form of NIBS, kilohertz transcranial magnetic perturbation (kTMP), in which a low frequency perturbation is created by the amplitude modulation (AM) of a continuous high-frequency carrier signal (3.5 kHz). As a magnetic induction method, kTMP can produce much higher electrical fields at the cortical surface than tACS and reduces cutaneous co-stimulation. Human participants (n=40) listened to sequences of rhythmic speech while receiving kTMP with an AM component of 3.125 Hz. The phasic modulation of perceptual sensitivity was greater during AM-kTMP than during sham stimulation, consistent with the hypothesis that AM-kTMP entrained neural activity underlying speech perception. Participants' ratings of rhythmic sensations and other side effects did not differ between AM-kTMP and sham stimulation. Together with its reduced peripheral stimulation, our results highlight kTMP as a promising NIBS method for modulating frequency-specific brain dynamics in speech perception.

item.title: Development of subcortical nuclei volume in utero over the second and third trimester.
item.description:
Brain imaging and behavior
Subcortical nuclei are important structures in the brain. Previous MRI evaluation of fetal brain development mostly focused on cerebral cortex and the myelination process, but few of them explored the developmental pattern of subcortical nuclei. The aim of this study is to analyze the developmental characteristics of fetal subcortical nuclei and their relationship with gestational age and cortical development. In this retrospective study, the precise axial, sagittal, and coronal views of T2-weighted brain MRI sequences in 47 fetuses with normal brains in the gestational age (GA) range of 22 to 36 weeks were obtained. A single 3D motion-corrected high-resolution brain volume was reconstructed from the 2D SSTSE imaging stacks using a slice-to-volume reconstruction (SVR) method. The volumes of the subcortical nuclei, i.e., amygdala, caudate, pallidum, putamen, hippocampus, subthalamic nucleus, thalamus, and cortex were segmented and corrected based on the above 3D images. We drew the developmental curve of each subcortical nucleus with age. The Pearson correlation coefficients were calculated between volumes of subcortical nuclei, as well as between volumes of cortical and subcortical regions, to explore how cortical regions and subcortical nuclei matured cooperatively. We illustrated the developmental trajectory curves of volumes of six subcortical nuclei and one of subcortical structure (thalamus, amygdala, hippocampus, caudate, putamen, subthalamic nucleus, and pallidum) according to the changes in GA to show the development trajectory of subcortical nuclei at 22-36 weeks. We further illustrated that volumes of subcortical nuclei and subcortical structure increased nonlinearly with GA, and the velopmental trajectories indicated laterality in the subcortical nuclei of the fetal brain. In addition, we found insignificant maturational coupling between subcortical nuclei and cortical regions, whereas the degree of maturational coupling between subcortical nuclei was relatively high. We found the volume of subcortical nuclei increased nonlinearly with the increase of GA, and the trajectory of nuclear mass development was lateral. The patterns of nuclear cluster development could expand our understanding of the brain growth. Reference ranges of fetal intracranial structures across gestational ages can serve as a valuable adjunct to prenatal counseling when interpreted in conjunction with clinical context and ultrasound findings.

item.title: Influence of regional white matter lesion volume differences related to cardiorespiratory fitness on cognition in healthy older adults.
item.description:
GeroScience
Greater cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) has been associated with reduced global burden of white matter hyperintensity (WMH) lesions, a neuroimaging marker of small vessel cerebrovascular disease, and lower risk of age-related cognitive impairment and dementia. However, little is known about how CRF relates to regional patterns of WMH volume and the associated impact on cognitive aging. In a cohort of 166 community-dwelling, healthy older adults (mean age = 70.49 ± 9.96 years, 48.8% women), we investigated the association of CRF with regionally distributed WMH burden using multivariate regional network analysis of hemispheric lobar WMH volumes. We additionally evaluated the moderating role of CRF-related regional WMH volumetric differences for cognition. Higher CRF, distinct from self-reported habitual physical activity, was associated with a distributed covariance pattern of WMH volume reductions in bilateral frontal and right parietal lobes, with relative increases in bilateral occipital lobes. Greater CRF-WMH pattern expression was associated with younger age and male sex. Additionally, there was a significant age-by-CRF-WMH network pattern interaction for memory, but not for information processing speed and executive functioning, such that the higher the pattern expression, the weaker the inverse association between age and memory performance. Our findings suggest that having greater CRF may help to maintain cerebrovascular health in older adults as reflected in its association with reduced WMH burden in regions particularly vulnerable to brain aging and associated memory dysfunction. Multivariate CRF-WMH pattern expression may provide a marker of cerebrovascular health that may help to identify those at increased risk for age-related cognitive impairment.

item.title: Whole-Brain Dynamics and Cognitive Flexibility in Level 1 ASD: An HMM-Based Approach.
item.description:
Journal of autism and developmental disorders
Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a complex neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by differences in cognitive flexibility, which are closely associated with restricted and repetitive behaviors (RRB). However, the dynamic brain network mechanisms underlying these differences remain poorly understood. This study investigated the neural correlates of cognitive flexibility difficulties in ASD by analyzing dynamic brain network features and explored their potential as diagnostic biomarkers. We applied hidden Markov models (HMMs) to resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data to characterize dynamic brain network states in children with ASD (n = 69) and typically developing (TD) children (n = 50). Cognitive flexibility was assessed using the Behavior Rating Inventory of Executive Function (BRIEF). An independent ABIDE II dataset was used for external validation. Machine learning models evaluated the diagnostic utility of behavioral and neuroimaging markers. Children with ASD showed atypical brain network dynamics, specifically a reduced brain state switching rate (p < 0.01) and asymmetric activation of the frontoparietal network (FPN). These alterations were significantly associated with cognitive flexibility difficulties and RRB severity in the ASD group (Benjamini-Hochberg FDR q < 0.05) and generalized to the independent sample. Combining cognitive flexibility scores with brain state switching rates yielded high diagnostic accuracy (internal AUC: 0.897 (95% CI 0.812-0.963); external AUC: 0.869 (95% CI 0.781-0.943)). This study provides novel insights into the dynamic neural mechanisms underlying cognitive flexibility differences in ASD. The findings support combined behavioral and neuroimaging biomarkers for improving ASD diagnosis and lay the groundwork for individualized intervention research.

item.title: Network Control Theory in Psychiatry: From Connectivity-Derived Controllability to Brain-State Transitions and Interventions.
item.description:
Neuroscience and biobehavioral reviews
Psychiatric disorders are increasingly conceptualized as disruptions in brain dynamics, particularly in how activity patterns evolve over time. Network Control Theory (NCT), a framework derived from control engineering, has emerged as a promising approach for studying these dynamics. Yet, despite its growing application in psychiatry, it remains unclear whether NCT has provided mechanistic or clinical insights beyond conventional measures of network topology. Here, we conducted a PRISMA-guided systematic review of NCT applications across major psychiatric disorders in adults. Of 178 records identified, 26 studies met inclusion criteria, representing 17 unique cohorts spanning schizophrenia spectrum disorders, major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, obsessive-compulsive disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder. Across studies, a recurring pattern of lower modal controllability was reported in several disorders (3 independent cohorts), although regional findings were heterogeneous and diagnostic specificity was limited. In contrast, task-based analyses under cognitive load (2 cohorts) and energy-based metrics (2 cohorts), though scarce, revealed more extensive case-control abnormalities and between-disorder differentiation. Intervention studies provided preliminary evidence that NCT-derived measures may predict treatment response and inform individualized neuromodulation targets (4 cohorts). However, 21 of 26 studies exclusively relied on connectivity-derived controllability metrics that were closely related to conventional measures of network topology and characterized model-implied control properties rather than directly observed state transitions. Furthermore, translational evidence came largely from single-arm, retrospective and simulation studies. The distinct value of NCT in psychiatry therefore remains to be established. Future progress requires the use of empirically observed brain states, energy-based measures, and prospective intervention studies.

item.title: Combined Neuromelanin-Sensitive and Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging Links Midbrain Dopaminergic Dysfunction to Connectome Architecture in First-Episode, Medication-Naïve Major Depressive Disorder.
item.description:
Biological psychiatry
Background Accumulating evidence implicates dopaminergic dysfunction in major depressive disorder (MDD), yet direct evidence of such dysfunction and of its altered coupling with the functional connectome remains limited. Methods Using neuromelanin-sensitive MRI (NM-MRI) and resting-state fMRI, we examined differences in substantia nigra/ventral tegmental area NM-MRI signal (NMSSN/VTA ) between first-episode, medication-naïve MDD patients (n = 112) and healthy controls (HC; n = 230). Network-based statistics (NBS) assessed MDD-related alterations in NMSSN/VTA -functional connectivity (FC) coupling. Spatial correspondence analyses examined the spatial convergence of these coupling alterations with normative dopaminergic molecular maps and anhedonia-related connectome patterns in MDD. Results Patients with MDD showed lower NMSSN/VTA , with more pronounced reductions in lateral and rostral regions. NBS identified a widespread component with altered NMSSN/VTA -FC coupling in MDD, characterized predominantly by higher slopes across attention, control, sensory, and medial temporal systems and lower slopes involving limbic-striatal and default-mode connections. Network-level analysis further identified a diagnosis-dependent NMSSN/VTA -striatal-limbic connectivity relationship, with lower NMSSN/VTA associated with higher FC in MDD. Spatially, these coupling alterations converged with dopaminergic molecular architecture, showing negative correspondence with normative dopaminergic receptor and transporter distributions and positive correspondence with the anticipatory-pleasure-related connectome pattern in MDD. Conclusions These findings provide in vivo evidence of midbrain dopaminergic dysfunction and widespread disruption of dopaminergic-connectome coupling in MDD, with these coupling alterations spatially converging with anhedonia-related connectome organization. Together, these findings advance our understanding of the role of dopaminergic dysfunction in the pathophysiology of MDD.
